1.point: Open with the Munajat's unusual plea for forgiveness and say that this chapter covers the first stage: repentance, kept steady, then the law kept strictly, starting with people.
steps: A hook: the Munajat asks forgiveness not for a particular sin but for a life spent forgetting God.
That plea is where the road begins; it opens the first of Chapter Eight's four stages (polishing).
State the chapter's three claims: anyone can begin by repenting; repentance is kept at a steady pace; the law is kept strictly, beginning with how we treat people.

2.point: The road starts with repentance, and because repentance covers every sin and every wrong attitude, no sinner is shut out of it.
steps: Setting out is two moves: wake up, then repent; repentance is the first step of the road.
Repentance here is wider than sin: it is repenting from casualness towards God.
So it is open to the sinner as much as to the devout; early mystics began as wrongdoers (Fudayl).
What stops sinners is not sin but despair that the road is for better people.
The Qur'an answers that despair: God forgives all sins, so no believer may set the road aside.
Land it: anyone can begin, and the Munajat gives words that any believer can say.

3.point: Repentance is renewed whenever the traveller falls, taken no faster than the self can bear, and not put off to old age.
steps: Old habits return; the traveller repents again, so repentance is continuous.
They return because the self fights back at every stage and can strike hard.
Therefore rushing is dangerous: pushed beyond its basis, the self gives way and the traveller falls.
Illustration: the Tehran friend told to stop Ziyarat Ashura because he was rushing without basis; the Imams' counsel of one step at a time.
But steady is not slow: putting the road off to old age is its own despair and only makes it harder.
Land it: steady pace means renewed, not rushed, not postponed.

4.point: The rest of the first stage is keeping the law strictly, and the first thing the law demands of the traveller is putting relations with people right.
steps: Polishing is keeping what the Prophet ordered in the strictest sense; no one passes to the next stage without it.
Within the law, one condition comes first: conduct towards people; without it no practice moves the traveller forward.
The reason is the system of justice: any wrong done to anyone, even unknowingly, holds the traveller back until it is put right.
What this conduct looks like: the Prophet and Imams stayed friendly with everyone at the summit, and it reaches down to the smallest courtesy (Hatim al-Asamm).
Land it: polishing begins with repentance and continues as the law, whose first demand is people.

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: The hook: sets the Munajat's plea against habitual istighfar and names what it confesses (a life of forgetting God). Nothing earlier supplies this.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Links the plea to the road, recalls Chapter Eight's four stages in one sentence and states the chapter's three claims. This is the section's job and it does it.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Supplies the first step: wake, then repent; repentance is the first step of the road, with Khomeini confirming the order.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Supplies the second step: repentance here is wider than sin (casualness towards God), with the Lantern distinction between elite and common repentance. ¶5's 'covers every sin and every wrong attitude' depends on it.

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: Draws the consequence: because it covers everything, it is open to sinners as to the devout, and gives the early wrongdoers as proof. Sets up the Fudayl box.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Supplies the real obstacle: not sin but despair that the road belongs to a higher calibre. Introduces the verse that answers it.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Applies the verse: 'excesses against their own souls' includes wasted capacity, God forgives all, so the verse is an encouragement to begin. This is the step that removes the obstacle ¶6 raised.

¶8.label: aside
¶8.why: The point is that anyone can begin; that God loves the penitent and that repentance burnishes the heart are further benefits of repentance, not steps to the point. Nothing later uses them (¶9's 'therefore' follows from ¶7, not ¶8). The one salvageable line is the last, which explains why repentance belongs to a stage called polishing; it would sit better in ¶21.

¶9.label: advance
¶9.why: Lands the conclusion and closes the frame by bringing the Munajat back with words a penitent sinner can say. First statement of the conclusion in the section.

¶10.label: restate
¶10.why: Glosses the quotation, but 'sinner and penitent at once' was already said in ¶9 and 'any believer can say' is the conclusion again. A second statement of the point.

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: First step of the section: habits return, the traveller repents again, repentance is continuous.

¶12.label: aside
¶12.why: A second authority with a stricter standard, set 'side by side' with the first and left there. The tension is raised and not resolved, no later paragraph uses it, and ¶20's conclusion is built on ¶11, ¶14 and ¶19 only. It also muddies the section's word 'steady' (pace) with Tabataba'i's 'steadiness' (never again).

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Supplies why habits return: the self fights back at every stage and can strike hard. ¶14's 'Because the self can strike back' depends on it.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Draws the step the point needs: rushing is dangerous because the self cannot carry it; names the Imams' pace and introduces the story.

¶15.label: support
¶15.why: First half of the story ¶14 announced; ¶16 draws the lesson from it.

¶16.label: support
¶16.why: Completes the story and states its lesson ('you need to have basis'), plus the three-month fast comparison. Evidence for ¶14's claim, which ¶20 then uses.

¶17.label: support
¶17.why: Pays ¶14's promise of 'the pace the Imams advised' with the ladder hadith. On its own the hadith is about not burdening others; it only bears on one's own pace through ¶18's reading, so the pair stands or falls together.

¶18.label: aside
¶18.why: A second scholar making the same point as ¶14-16 (do not rush) with a second mechanism (burnout rather than a fall). The point does not need two mechanisms and ¶20 uses only the first ('no faster than the self can bear'). If cut, ¶17 should be trimmed to the one sentence ¶14 needs or go with it.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Supplies the other half of the point: not rushing is not postponing; age limits ability, not mercy. New step, nothing earlier covers it.

¶20.label: restate
¶20.why: A summary of ¶11, ¶14 and ¶19. It is the section's landing, but ¶19 already ends on the sooner-the-easier line and could carry the close.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Supplies the first step: polishing is keeping the law in the strictest sense and no one passes the stage without it. Recalls Chapter Six in one sentence.

¶22.label: advance
¶22.why: Supplies the second step: within the law, the first condition is conduct towards people; without it no practice moves the traveller.

¶23.label: advance
¶23.why: Supplies the reason: the system of justice holds a traveller back for any wrong, even unknowing, until it is put right.

¶24.label: aside
¶24.why: The 'therefore' does no work: ¶23 already gave the reason the road cannot go around people. This offers a second reason from a second authority (good conduct is the core of the message) and nothing later uses it.

¶25.label: support
¶25.why: Shows what the demand looks like at the top of the road (the Prophet and Imams friendly with all) and introduces the Nahj description. ¶26's 'Good conduct of this kind' refers back to it.

¶26.label: support
¶26.why: Extends the example to its smallest case and introduces the Hatim box; ¶27's 'down to sparing an ordinary person's embarrassment' uses it.

¶27.label: restate
¶27.why: Summarises Sections 2, 3 and 4. Each of its sentences has already been stated as a conclusion (¶9, ¶20, ¶21-22).

¶28.label: aside
¶28.why: First sentence restates ¶9; the second raises a question the chapter does not answer. The argument uses neither.
